subsubtopic: OMISSION OF QUEEN'S PORTRAIT FROM POSTAGE STAMPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, is Canada Post going republican? When the new 36cent stamps were issued in April many were disappointed to
discover that there was none bearing the Queen's portrait. This stamp was promised twice for dates in May but still has not appeared. Many Toronto customers have been told by post office workers there that it might never be issued.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF MAINTENANCE SHOPS IN WINNIPEG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a controversy broke out a week or so ago about the announcement which the Minister of Transport made in the House that VIA Rail would now be free to go ahead with constructing the maintenance shops in Winnipeg, Vancouver, and Halifax which were postponed when the Conservatives came to office. The controversy was with regard to whether the plans for Winnipeg would be downgraded and the major western maintenance facility would be at Vancouver.
If VIA is considering downgrading the maintenance facility in Winnipeg, I want to tell the House, VIA, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), and anyone else concerned with this issue, from an operational point of view, that I advise it not to make the same mistakes as railways have made on occasion in the past, that is, try to run trains from Toronto in the east and Vancouver in the west to Winnipeg, turn them around there, and run them back without having the major maintenance facility in Winnipeg.
It is a fact of Canadian life, due to the climate, that equipment most often breaks down in Winnipeg, particularly in the winter. It would be sheer madness for VIA to differ from the plan of having Winnipeg as a major maintenance facility, both on the motive power side and on the coach side.

May 29, 1987

subtopic: S. O. 21 NARCOTICS NATIONAL DRUG STRATEGY-SUPPORT FOR GOVERNMENT PROGRAM
S. O. 21 NARCOTICS NATIONAL DRUG STRATEGY-SUPPORT FOR GOVERNMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last fall the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced plans to deal with Canada's drug epidemic. This is a problem which affects in some way virtually every family in Canada, a problem which not only costs the nation millions in lost productivity, but also threatens the minds and lives of many Canadians. In combatting drug abuse the state clearly has a place in the classrooms, workrooms and boardrooms of the nation.
This week the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) put forward a $210 million five-year plan which will involve public education, drug and alcohol treatment and rehabilitation, law enforcement and control, and research efforts.
I congratulate the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, first for recognizing that there is a drug crisis in Canada, second, for undertaking to educate all Canadians about the dangers of drug abuse and, third, for responding in a number of concrete ways; internationally through our consulates abroad, and domestically in cooperation with the provinces and community groups.

Mr. Speaker, the aboriginal leaders of Canada and the people whom they represent feel betrayed by the Meech Lake Accord. They, too, have sought to have their distinct place in Canada recognized in our Constitution. Repeatedly, however, they have been rebuffed by fearful, hesitant Premiers who seek more power for themselves but are unwilling to share even a modest amount with others.
The second round of constitutional talks referred to in the Accord mentions fisheries, but aboriginal rights are left out. This is an omission of enormous proportions. The fishery and aboriginal rights are intimately related. I, therefore, urge the inclusion of aboriginal peoples and their rights on the second round agenda.
In the Yukon and Northwest Territories court action is under way against the Meech Lake Accord. To give every Premier a veto over the creation of new provinces is highly offensive to the Governments of the North and the northerners whom they represent.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL UNITY-IMPACT OF VISIT BY PRESIDENT OF FRANCE-GOVERNMENT'S PERFORMANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this week, I commented on President Mitterand's visit to Canada, and today, a few hours before he leaves this country, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the positive impact of this brief visit.
I want to point out the general approval surrounding the cordial welcome the President received. The unanimity of Canadians in this respect reflects the unity of this country.
As a Canadian, I am particularly happy to feel this unity, since all Canadians want to live in a united Canada. This country has not always been as united, but since we came to power in 1984, our Prime Minister has managed to create this climate of national unity, a fact of which Canadians are very proud.
In concluding, I would like to repeat what I said Tuesday, namely, that the positive impact of President Mitterand's visit will continue to make itself felt and that the prospects for a united Canada under Prime Minister Mulroney are very good indeed.

Mr. Speaker, Statistics Canada has just published some very encouraging material showing the important entry of women into the professions. There has been a great change in representation, especially in the professions of law and pharmacy. We welcome that change.
In the case of engineering the increase is in the order of 300 per cent. However, since the figure has only risen from 1 per cent to 3 per cent it is not very encouraging. We need to see more storming of these all-male bastions, these boys clubs in the engineering schools.
Canada can only be a great country if its people are well trained. We need the talents of all our people. Thus we welcome this important development of women moving into the professions.
We have to support concrete measures to see that this movement continues. I hope that it will be matched by the movement of native peoples, handicapped persons, and people of visible minorities so that we will have really fair representation and that, as a country, we will be able to employ the talents of all our people.
May 29, 1987

subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA DAIRY INDUSTRY-IMPORTATION OF DUTYFREE PRODUCTS FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the dairy industry of British Columbia is deeply worried about the volume of milk and dairy products that is being brought into British Columbia from the U.S. without duty charged.
Customs officials at the five Lower Mainland crossings have calculated that on a daily average there are 12,200 cars crossing at these borders and that 65 per cent to 80 per cent of individuals returning home to B.C. through four of these crossings have purchased dairy products. At the Point Roberts crossing the estimate is that 100 per cent bring home these goods. This crossing, which is U.S. territory, is accessible only through Canada and has been called the "milk and gas run".
If we consider that each car has an average of 2.5 people in it and that each person represents $10 Canadian of dairy products, this could add up to a staggering $72 million per year lost to the B.C. dairy industry. Small grocery stores have opened along the Washington border to sell milk, eggs and bread to Canadian customers who just "pop across the border".
The 17 per cent duty that the law requires is not needed on "small value" grocery items. I believe that Customs must enforce this levy in order to ensure that Canadian dairy producers will receive the full protection of our excise law.

Mr. Speaker, the people of Montreal have been waiting a long time for the Old Port of Montreal, to be developed. Once it has been developed, the Old Port will have much to contribute to the city, in terms of beauty, recreation and tourism. However, as in the case of the space agency, the Conservative Government has been dragging its feet. Montreal has been waiting nearly three years for financial assistance to develop the Old Port. The city of Toronto made a similar request, and it did receive funding. Will the Old Port of Montreal have the same fate as the space agency?
Yesterday, a telegram was sent to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes), and to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), signed by Mrs. Manon Vennat and Mr. Marcel Daoust of the Montreal Chamber of Commerce. In it the federal Government is asked to provide funding for the development of the Port of Montreal.
I therefore want to add my voice to that of my colleagues and I ask the Government to act quickly.

subsubtopic: SUCCESS OF ALBERTA'S TRIPLICATE PRESCRIPTION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Alberta the College of Physicians and Surgeons introduced the triplicate prescription program one year ago. Chemical addiction is a principal disease of our time and prescription drug abuse plays a major role.
For the 10 most commonly abused drugs, narcotics and others, the physician uses a special prescription pad with an original and two copies, keeping the original for himself. The patient then takes two copies to the pharmacist who sends one to the college.
Using computers, the college can identify a physician who is providing unusual amounts of these drugs and patients who may be going from doctor to doctor for prescriptions. If several doctors are involved, they are notified and then are in a position to treat their patients more effectively if addiction is indicated. It is a true success story.
In commending the Alberta College of Physicians and Surgeons along with the Alberta Government, and the Alberta Pharmaceutical Association which support this initiative, I urge the federal Government to make this a national program.

Mr. Speaker, the Governments of Yukon and the Northwest Territories have launched a suit in the Supreme Court regarding the Meech Lake Accord. Canadians north of 60 have aspirations to provincehood just as did our forefathers in each of the 10 provinces.
Prior to the 1982 Constitution Act, provinces were created bilaterally between the federal Government and the region wishing status. In these intervening five years, the requirement has been the general amending formula of seven provinces with 50 per cent of the population, along with Parliament.
The Meech Lake Accord touches on the creation of new provinces and provincial boundaries in a most fundamental sense by requiring the unanimity of provinces. I have reviewed the public record and find no evidence of provinces, federal Parties, or public groups arguing for the application of unanimity for the creation of new provinces. This raises a fundamental constitutional and political question that must be addressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
Since there has been no debate upon applying such a measure, Canadians must ask why and on what grounds are the aspirations of northerners to be made so much more

subsubtopic: TAKEOVER OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AIR-LOSS OF JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is with regard to the takeover of Canadian Pacific Air by Pacific Western Airlines. It is now obvious that the Government did not know what it was doing when it approved the takeover. The Government was either innocently naive or grossly incompetent when it deemed that particular takeover to be in the best interests of Canada.
On March 25 the Government estimated that 3,000 jobs would be lost as a result of the takeover. On April 2 it said that few if any jobs would be lost. Today we learned from the president of the new airline that up to 1,900 jobs will be lost as a result of the takeover.
1 will direct my question to the Minister responsible. Why did the Government approve the takeover when it knew, or ought to have known, that so many jobs would be lost? Is this what airline deregulation is all about?

subsubtopic: TAKEOVER OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AIR-LOSS OF JOBS

Mr. Speaker, as usual my friend opposite is entirely incorrect. The effect of deregulation, which was started by his Party, has, on an over-all basis, been an increase in the number of Canadians working in the airline industry. It is true that in this particular merger there will perhaps be a loss of up to 1,900 jobs. However, most of those losses will be handled through attrition, the golden handshake, and reorganization. However, we should always remember that on an overall basis there will be more people working in the airline industry as a result of deregulation than there were when the Liberals had everything tightly regulated.

subsubtopic: UNITED STATES TRANS-BOUNDARY ACID RAIN EMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs who, I am sure, will answer it in his usual non-partisan manner. It has to do with the fact that in January of this year the Minister of the Environment called upon the United States to reduce trans-boundary acid rain emissions by half by 1994. Last week, after Canadian and U.S. officials met in Washington, they indicated that the Government of Canada has become flexible, that it is not going to demand what the Minister of the Environment called for in January.
Why does the Government appear to give up its bargaining position at the very first meeting in Washington?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES TRANS-BOUNDARY ACID RAIN EMISSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I try to provide non-partisan answers to non-partisan questions. Let me see if I can find a non-partisan element in that question. Perhaps the best way would be to indicate that at the most recent meeting, which was designed in part to try to make some progress towards formalizing the reference the President of the United States made here on the floor of the House of Commons to some kind of formal agreement, we think that some progress was made. We have learned not to celebrate that progress until it has been achieved. However, I think the House will recognize, in fairness, that there has been some modest movement forward on the part of the United States administration on this very serious question of acid rain. Certainly we believe it is important to continue that process rather than to walk away in frustration from the talks.

subsubtopic: UNITED STATES TRANS-BOUNDARY ACID RAIN EMISSIONS
speechtext: I am so glad that the Secretary of State for External Affairs refrained from rounding off his final sentence and 1 appreciate the thoughtfulness of his answer.

Will the Secretary of State for External Affairs assure this House now that the Government of Canada will not waver in its position as expounded by the Minister of the Environment last November, namely, that it will not abandon the position of demanding from the U.S. a cut by half in trans-boundary acid rain emissions by 1994?
May 29, 1987

We intend to continue to seek a reduction in trans-boundary emissions. We require not only constancy on the part of the Government, which will continue to be there, but support and constancy on the part of parliamentarians who have taken an active interest in this issue.
I have been informed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, that the Parliamentary Committee on Acid Rain will be in Washington later in June. I think the Hon. Member will be part of that group. I certainly hope they can contribute in a constructive way in trying to achieve a reduction in trans-boundary emissions, which is the goal of this Government.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, May 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hockin that Bill C-42, an Act respecting financial institutions and the deposit insurance system, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
1 rise to make a few comments on Bill C-42 in order to review the policy direction that the Government is proposing with respect to this Bill and to show how we arrived at this point. Since this is second reading debate such comments, 1 understand, are appropriate.
The proposal that we are dealing with here today comes in part out of the Estey report which came about because of the failure of two of our financial institutions, namely, the Northland Bank and the Canadian Commercial Bank. During the same period of time, we saw a number of federal and provincial trust and loan institutions and some casualty insurance companies collapse. When the totals were added up,
1 believe that something like two banks collapsed in 1985; since 1980, nine trust and loan companies collapsed, and again since 1980, five property and casualty insurance companies collapsed.
All of this raised serious doubts about the ability of the regulatory package that had been in place since the collapse in 1923 of the Home Bank to handle the four pillars of our financial institutions. That collapse, along with the depression of the 1930s, resulted in a series of regulatory proposals that had the effect of establishing traditional areas of function for banks, trust companies, insurance companies and the securities industry. Each was complete in itself, and separate, and there was very little integration of the four pillars. Some people believe that a fifth pillar has been established by way of the cooperative credit institutions which have become a force in the financial services area.
The intention of the legislative and regulatory program was to establish, as a result of what occurred in the 1930s, such departments for regulation and supervision as the Department of Insurance, which looked after insurance companies, the Inspector General of Banks, responsible for regulating and monitoring the banks and the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation, which provides guarantees to depositors of $60,000 per depositor. Out of that same set of changes came the Bank of Canada, to provide last-minute funding to keep banking institutions as viable as possible.
Over the years these regulatory commissions appear to have been doing their jobs. We had no problems until the 1980s,

May 29, 1987
Financial Institutions
and then we were faced with this sudden and unexpected collapse of the two banks which precipitated the Estey Inquiry. At the same time, something like nine trust and loan companies and five casualty and property insurance companies collapsed. The question of whether or not our financial institutions were being properly monitored and regulated came into public view.
Internationally, there was a philosophical move toward complete deregulation of these kinds of institutions. We saw this happening in Great Britain under the Conservative Government of Margaret Thatcher, and we saw considerable deregulation under the similar-minded administration of President Reagan in the United States.
Perhaps as a result of this, there was beginning to be a tendency for those clear functions of the four or five pillars to blur together. Insurance programs were being introduced by some banking institutions, and mortgage and trust company functions were being carried out by all of the pillars. Some Canadians feared that the blurring and intermarriage of these companies was responsible in part for the difficulty the Inspector General of Banks and the Inspector of Insurance had in carrying out their regulatory and supervisory functions.
While the international philosophical move was away from regulation, this Bill, after the Estey report, appears to be trying to make a compromise between continued regulation or reregulation and lip service toward deregulation as well. The report submitted by Justice Estey in October of 1986 provided the basis for the White Paper which was produced on financial institution reform. I would like to very quickly go through some of the Government's proposals embodied in its twin aims of deregulation and reregulation. I will try to keep it brief as 1 know that our time is limited to 20 minutes.
The Government is proposing to allow the diversification and integration of financial services within the total industry so that consumers will be able to deposit and withdraw funds, buy stocks and bonds, arrange loans and mortgages and obtain investment advice and portfolio management, all within the walls of one branch of a financial institution. For instance, banks will be able to underwrite securities while trust and loan and insurance companies will enjoy full consumer and commercial lending privileges. To a certain extent, these kinds of services are beginning to be offered by some companies already, even though the regulations have not changed.
Having been a Member of Parliament only since 1980, I have observed that this seems to be the pattern with very large financial institutions. 1 recall that when the Bank Act came up for revision in 1980, we rescinded the Usury Act which would have limited interest rates lending institutions could charge. As a new Member, 1 was somewhat appalled and surprised that the actual rate of interest charged by most of the financial institutions had for some months exceeded the limit in the Usury Act and no charges had been laid and nothing was done. Instead, the Government chose to simply rescind the Act and change the law so that the practice would become legal.
To a certain extent, that kind of thing is now occurring as the clear distinctions between the functions of the four pillars has eroded. 1 fear that to some extent this Bill may be a reaction to the existing erosion. 1 only raise this fear because 1 think Members of Parliament, in their blind and simple way of looking at things, would hope that practices in Canada would conform to the law as lorjg as the law is in effect. While I know society changes and politicians often respond after the changes have occurred, we should always be conscious of compliance with the law and we should provide ways to make certain that compliance.
I believe that was one of the difficulties that emerged with the two banks that collapsed. As 1 recall, it appeared that the Inspector General of Banks did not have sufficient resources and personnel to do the job of inspection and to provide the proper kinds of information required by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) or the Minister responsible for these institutions, depending on how the Government decided to set things up.
Some of these shortcomings may in fact continue with this proposal, since a new office will be set up, that of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. 1 understand that it would combine, more or less, the Inspector General of Banks and the functions of the Superintendent of Insurance. This combined office would be given a new title, that of Superintendent of Financial Institutions.
The information we have at this point would indicate that the resources available to that office would not be much greater than the combined resources of the existing institutions. In fact, I am wondering whether the interests of consumers will be well served and whether the institution will be well monitored.
Given the now blurred functions of the various institutions, I suspect that it will be more difficult to track down the various combinations of responsibility, ownership, and commitment among various like-minded institutions which, at one time, were clearly separate and apart and therefore more easily monitored and regulated.
The principle of deposit insurance has been under some attack as a result of the bail-out of the Northland Bank and the Canadian Commercial Bank which went under in 1985. Several proposals have been put forward which would basically fall into two categories. The first proposition put forward is that uninsured depositors should be responsible for carrying the burden of a failure of an institution. The other extreme, 1 suppose, was to make certain that all deposits were fully insured and that over a certain level-and 1 assume it would be the $60,000 which was proposed as the maximum level of complete insurance-depositors would pay a higher share of deposit insurance so that almost full coverage of deposits would be possible if a bank or financial institution in fact failed. These kinds of propositions are floating around.
May 29, 1987

Bill C-42 seems to be fairly unambitious in its treatment of the problem. The Bill gives Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation a closer relationship with other regulatory officials and a procedure by which it can terminate deposit insurance coverage for recalcitrant institutions. In the case of this happening, a registered letter delivered to the institution's chief executive would be sent out detailing CD1C complaints. The institution's board must then convene and send a report to CDIC on its deliberations within a given time period.
If CDIC remains dissatisfied it can, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, terminate insurance coverage within 30 days of notice. The procedure will take some time, but there is enough time involved that it is very difficult to intervene quickly enough if there are some shenanigans ongoing within the corporation.
Bill C-42 also attempts to deal with the present debt of CDIC, which I understand is somewhere around $1.5 billion, by increasing the fees for deposit insurance. They will be set at $5,000 per institution, plus one-sixth of one percent of each deposit held by the institution. Most financial institutions have responded to the Government's proposal, including the top five chartered banks, by strongly objecting to this solution and citing the issue of uninsured deposit coverage. Apparently they are still attempting to negotiate the particular issue.
Since the time for my remarks is almost over, I should like to point out that it has been the position of the New Democratic Party that the problem of financial institutional solvency can be resolved only through a combination of clear and effective regulatory and supervisory controls for financial institutions in Canada, with strict domestic ownership limits which ensure that institutions will be widely held. This is one issue which has been debated at some length in financial and policy areas.
Upon entering this new era, some institutions will hold as much as 35 per cent of another institution, which normally would have been one of the other competing pillars of the financial institution under the old analysis.
A great many of us think that it should be limited to about 10 per cent per investor, so that there will be in effect a discouragement in respect of the controlling of some companies, even though only 35 per cent of the shares are held.
We would prefer that the 35 per cent be reduced to 10 per cent by law in order to make certain that financial, insurance, and trust company institutions in Canada are as widely held as possible, to avoid the kind of control and manipulation which appears to have occurred in some of the provincial scandals involving trust and loan companies with fast flips and that sort of thing. We would hope that these kinds of amendments could be made to the process, if not in this particular Bill, in companion Bills which deal more specifically with that particular aspect.
I conclude by saying that we will be watching the legislation closely and will be attempting to make appropriate amendments to bring about the kind of regulatory reform which we
Financial Institutions
in the New Democratic Party believe would be in the best interests of Canadian users of financial insurance institutions.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-42 is an Act respecting financial institutions and the deposit insurance system. Because of the general importance of the subject, both to many Canadians as individual investors and to all Canadians who must be concerned about the possible dangers to our economy if mismanagement of large sums of money, it is quite important that something should be said on the matter, and 1 am glad of the opportunity to contribute to the debate.
The legislation before us appears to be fairly good, as far as it goes, but it appears that it does not go far enough. Of course the concern is with the conflict between the Government's interest in deregulating financial institutions and what even it recognizes as the failure, to date, of some of the regulatory activities, and perhaps some of the regulatory legislation. Therefore, the Government appears to be trying to steer a middle course and taking too cautious a line.
We had the very unfortunate collapse of two western banks a couple of years ago, apparently caused by unwise lending practices, unwise in the sense that they made bad loans because they thought they would get high interest, and their investors invested because of high interest. Then, when the banks collapsed, the investors demanded-and the Government agreed-that they be reimbursed even beyond what legislation at that time required in the form of loan insurance. That has given the Government a very difficult situation to deal with, and it does not seem to be able to think its way clearly to the end of the problem.
We had quite a spate of failures in the early 1980s in the loan and insurance company section of the business. There were two national bank failures in the mid 1980s. The Government has had to give attention to the matter of preventing further failures like those, since clearly people were in danger of losing their confidence in the banking system.
Canada has been lucky for over half a century in not having any serious troubles of that sort. The present legislation was mainly developed about 60 years ago after the collapse of the Home Bank in 1923, and further during the Great Depression. However, part of the principle adopted at that time is what is now being changed by the Government.
At that time there was an attempt to make sure that there was a spreading out of financial responsibility and power, a spreading out between lending institutions, deposit institutions, stocks and bonds institutions and insurance institutions. For the average person, some of those distinctions are hard to follow and to keep track of, especially as detailed regulations change. The principle was not to concentrate too much power in too few hands, which was what most people remembered as the results of the crash of 1929. Therefore, we have a system of controls, notably the Bank of Canada, the office of the Inspector General of Banks, the Department of Insurance, and

May 29, 1987
Financial Institutions
the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation with which many people are familiar because the CDIC has been called upon to act during several of these failures of banks or credit enterprises.
The situation has been complicated more recently by international development, particularly of conglomerates that combine these functions in ways that perhaps were not foreseen by earlier laws and sometimes are difficult to control because of their bases outside of Canada.
Britain and the United States are moving in the direction of deregulation of their financial enterprises. From time to time we see reports, particularly from the United States, about how paper money is growing mightily without very much counterpart in actual production of goods and services which ordinary people produce and need. In other words, takeovers, buy-outs, refinancings and so on can increase the paper value of an enterprise immensely without actually any more cars, food or any other goods or services being produced for the people who ultimately must carry the cost if the financial system collapses. There is a great deal of anxiety in the United States and Britain about what could happen when things get whirling at a faster and faster pace in the financial world without corresponding development in actual production.
The bank failures of 1985 might have prompted this Government to take more firm action than it seems minded to take in connection with controlling the banks. In 1986 because of the troubles in 1985, some of the smaller banks fell to the pressure of the distrust of the public, the distrust of the investors who are not in a position to know the intimate details of banks, even to the extent that the Inspector of Banks or the Bank of Canada are, and who may have been uneasy about their deposits in certain middle-sized banks, perhaps without good reason. They just did not know.
In 1986 the Mercantile Bank was forced to merge with the National Bank. The Morguard Bank, which I know was engaged in the 1970s in financing low-income housing built by the City of Toronto, and I think was serving a useful function, was taken over by the Security Pacific Bank. There was a Continental Bank that merged with Lloyds Bank of London through its Canadian subsidiary. There was recently the Bank of British Columbia which had to go somewhere. A local powerful financially strong credit union bid to buy that bank, but this Government and the crypto Tory Government of British Columbia desperately headed that off and, with the commitment of $200 million of taxpayers' money managed to ensure that a Canadian based democratically structured credit union did not gain control of the Bank of British Columbia; a foreign bank, the Hongkong Bank got it.
There have been a good many acquisitions of this sort which have considerably altered the general profile of the financial structures of our country placing much more power in much fewer hands. People are uneasy still about the solvency and the safety of an enterprise which is so remote from the control of the investors and perhaps remote from the control of the
Government which would have a responsibility and has the legislative power to take control.
When the western banks collapsed there was much discussion as to whether the controlling institutions, the Inspector of Banks and the Bank of Canada, had carried out their duties adequately or whether they were able to carry out their duties adequately. As these financial structures become more complicated, it becomes difficult to police them, as it were. When the managers make errors through excessive risk taking, through failing to match their assets and liabilities, through perhaps what is or may appear to be a conflict of interest, through self dealing, it is very difficult for the regulator agencies to keep up with, to keep watching all of them, or to keep doing enough inspections to keep track of these evolving institutions.
What happens then is that the officials who attempt to act decisively on behalf of the depositors, the policy holders, the creditors and other victims of the insolvency are hindered. They cannot act fast and surely enough to prevent the trouble such as wc witnessed in the bank collapses.
What we really need is a new framework-The Government has admitted this in its paper at the end of 1986-for corporate Governments to guide this institutional behaviour. Particularly, there have to be firm rules for self dealing and conflict of interest situations. It appears that that is where this Bill is very weak. We understand it is part of a package, but we are asked to take it on faith without being told clearly what the rest of that package will be. As I said, as far as it goes, it appears perhaps adequate.
There will be some development of the supervision powers of the Inspector General of Banks, the Department of Insurance, the Canada Insurance Corporation and the Bank of Canada. They will be given certain legal rights of control which go beyond what they have now. They will include the right of temporary seizing of assets of a troubled institution so as to give officials time to look into things and to respond to the complaints that have been made specifically about an institution's operations. Officials will be able to study the situation and, if they remain unconvinced that the institution really is solvent and will continue to be solvent, they can hold hearings with the Minister of Finance and the institution can afterwards be restricted. In effect, it can be supervised by the superintendent and if the institution fails to respond satisfactorily, the superintendent can wind up the business of the company.
The problem, as I say, is that apparently there is not enough muscle or enough money for staff to carry out this kind of investigation. The pressure on this regulatory institution to either leave them alone or act quickly will be such that the regulators will probably err on the side of leaving them alone, perhaps for too long as they did in the case of the western banks.
May 29, 1987

On the question of deposit insurance, which was a matter of hot public and parliamentary debate in connection with the western banks, it should be said that this protection of the public's investments is a very important element of a democratic banking sector. If small investors cannot be protected they will naturally hesitate to invest. The investment pool will then shrink and be occupied almost exclusively by the very large investors whose interests are not the same as small investors. Therefore it is understood to be in the interest of the country to have an insurance system which spreads the risk, within limits, and protects the ability of the small investor along with others to share in the direction of the investment industry.
Unfortunately, confidence in the insurance system was weakened when the Government decided to reimburse uninsured investors in the western banks. They were being reimbursed up to $60,000 according to the law, but the Government decided to reimburse them beyond that. In other words, it rewarded those who had acted foolishly and out of greed, whether it be the officers of the banks in question who made loans they should not have made because they hoped for unusually high returns, or whether it be the investors in those banks who made their investments for the same reason, being lured by high interest rates without examining sufficiently the basis on which the bank was operating.
In fact, Canadian taxpayers are still $1.5 billion in the hole for that bail-out. The Government is penny-pinching on unemployment insurance, pensions, children's allowances, funding of post-secondary education, social housing, even when it admits that half a million units are needed, yet it threw $1.5 billion to the richest people, not to the poorest people. They were protected by the law. It was the richest of the investors who got that $ 1.5 billion.
The provisions for controlling or revising the deposit insurance system seem a little uncertain or timid or tentative. It is not clear that there will be any firm prevention of the same kind of bad decisions. The banks that operate, not only within the law but within good investment practices and did not have to be bailed out, are now having to pay an extra levy in order to cover the Government's bail-out of the foolish banks. 1 understand that many banks are objecting to that practice.
What is lacking is a serious attempt to address the question of, as it were, cross-ownership in which a bank, insurance company or trust company may own a significant part of an enterprise to which it is also lending money. The NDP has for years advocated doing two things to provide reasonable insurance so that these financial enterprises can operate in reasonable safety. First, there has to be a combination of clear and effective regulations and supervision of the financial system. There is some movement in that direction in this Bill. Second, there has to be a restriction on this kind of crossownership, crossing over the lines of different sections of commercial and financial enterprises. There has to be restriction on ownership well below the present 35 per cent. We have
Financial Institutions
advocated the figure of 10 per cent. Without some restriction on that ownership and without a considerable increase in the funding of the regulatory institutions, which the Government has not offered and does not offer in this Bill, there is no serious and convincing control over the kind of crashes we have already seen and fear. Therefore I believe this Bill is not really fit to receive approval in principle.

Mr. Speaker, my friend from Spadina mentioned that small enterprises in his constituency have had a number of difficulties. I know of a restaurant in his riding, the proprietor of which was in constant battle with the bank branch in the area. The bank branch in turn could not get authority to make reasonable arrangements with the restaurant proprietor. They required an extraordinary amount of security including a mortgage on the home of the owner. Basically everything he owned was committed to maintaining this enterprise which was probably creating 10 or 15 jobs for people in the constituency of Spadina. This kind of story is repeated again and again.
How can this House of Commons make legislation which ensures that banks are stable for the Conrad Blacks, the Reichmanns and the Bronfmans of this world, are able to make substantial loans, some of which have turned out to be bad, to enterprises or governments, as a result of which enormous losses will be incurred and subsidized by the Canadian taxpayer, while ordinary citizens, farmers, consumers and small business people get pushed against the wall? What is fair about that? Why do we in the House of Commons, in studying the health and effectiveness of the banking system, which in some ways is very effective, not have as much concern for the needs of the little people, the consumers and farmers and so on, as we have for the stability of free enterprise? What use is there in having stable enterprises if they do not also provide effective service to the mass of Canadian citizens?

Small business people, would-be entrepreneurs, young people with education and ideas about modern technology, people skilled in computer work and so on, would like to try out their ideas and start their enterprises, but find a great lack of sympathy at the huge central bank offices at the bottom of

Spadina. They find an equal lack of sympathy at the branches on every corner.
There must be a greater sense of public accountability by the banks. It is good for the banks to be regulated so that they are not likely to fail and cause collapse. I would point out that when the Government subsidized; that is, bailed out the western banks with taxpayer's money, most of that money came from people who had not invested in those banks and probably did not have enough money to invest in those banks. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to move the second reading of Bill C-56, a measure which will bring important and necessary changes to federal legislation governing financial institutions. This Bill is, as we know, the second of three elements designed to strengthen the system of regulation of financial institutions and to implement the policy proposals which were announced on December 18.
The first element was introduced as Bill C-42, which was just referred to committee, and this Bill is the second.

The Bill regroups and amends two Bills that were tabled on October 6, 1986, and contains an important new provision that will allow federally regulated institutions to own brokerage firms.

All the measures introduced in the earlier Bills are included in this Bill. These include the power to review transfers and ownership of financial institutions, the power to issue cease and desist orders to institutions engaging in unsound or unsafe business practices, the very important power to revalue real estate assets and authority to strengthen the financial standards of insurance companies.
These measures, important as they are, have been in the public domain for several months. Bill C-9 was released in the form of draft legislation and comments which were received were reflected in the final Bill. The consultations indicated that there is wide-spread support for these measure. Bill C-8 also received wide-spread support from the insurance industry.
Major provisions in the Bill are as follows. First, with respect to transfers in ownership, the Bill would require that approval be obtained from the Minister of Finance when a company or individual wishes to acquire, directly or indirectly, an ownership position in a federally regulated trust, loan or insurance company that exceeds 10 per cent. That is a very important provision. The Bill provides for a process which must be followed by the Minister and the applicant when a transfer in ownership is contemplated and gives the Governor in Council the authority to prescribe the type of information which the prospective purchaser must file with the regulator in seeking approval.
Financial Institutions
By setting out a formal approval process for transfers in ownership, the Bill provides the basis for the implementation of the policy presented in the December 18 statement and, as you know, Mr. Speaker, the policy, in particular, was to arrest the formation of, or the increase in financial-commercial links. The latter would include any increases in ownership of financial institutions already held by commercially linked institutions or holding companies. Legislation to implement the remainder of the ownership rules, including the requirement that 35 per cent of the shares of commercially linked companies or large financial institutions be widely held and publicly traded, is expected this summer.
The second part of the Bill is very important, and that is in regard to cease and desist orders. The Bill would give the federal regulator the power to issue cease and desist orders to institutions engaging or planning to engage in any activity that is considered to be an unsafe or unsound business practice. In our discussion with respect to Bill C-42, expressions of concern, invoked by memories of the collapse of the two banks a few years ago, gives rise once again to the importance of having this power.
In the past, regulators have indicated that even when they were aware that unsafe or unsound business practices were being followed they frequently lacked the legislative authority to order the institution to cease the questionable practices. It was of great concern. They were watching this go on but there was no legislative authority to bring about the cessation of it. The cease and desist powers in this Bill are broad ranging and will respond to the need for both timely and effective intervention by the regulator.
The third part of the Bill is with respect to real estate valuation power. All of us who have seen how real estate values have changed during the 1980s will know this is important. No one who looks at the reform of financial institutions should overlook how they are often intricately related to real estate because it is such an important part of the assets of financial institutions.
The Bill would give the superintendent the power to prescribe values for real estate or assets secured by real estate held by federally incorporated trust, loan and insurance companies. Past experience has indicated that these companies can encounter serious problems from unrealistic real estate asset valuations. The valuation power will be an important measure in maintaining the public's confidence in our financial institutions.
The next major part of this legislation is to strengthen financial standards for insurance companies.

The Bill will substantially increase the financial standards that insurance companies must meet and will introduce further measures to strengthen the industry.

Financial Institutions

For life insurance companies, the Bill would authorize the setting of minimum continuing capital and surplus margins by regulation or by written ministerial directive. The proposed provision follows the precedent in the Bank Act in this regard. The provision would, for the first time, make life insurers subject to statutory minimum capital and surplus margins on an ongoing basis. Other financial institutions are already subject to legislative provisions in this area. I think the House knows that minimum capital requirements are crucial for trust companies and banks since that is the number on which all this leverage is based. Since we are allowing insurance companies to move into these new areas of power we had to put this capital provision in place, something which is at the very heart of a financial institution.
For property and casualty insurers the Bill provides for an increase in the minimum continuing capital, or solvency, requirements. Our major influence as the federal Government in the field of property and casualty insurance is really in the area of solvency. That is the reason people look to us, to make judgments on solvency.
Also, property and casualty insurance companies would be required to submit actuarial reports with their annual statements. These reports must contain a professional opinion with regard to the adequacy of reserves established to provide for future claims under policies in force and to cover the costs of claims that have occurred but are not yet paid. This provision would adopt a practice long used with considerable success in connection with life insurers. The new requirement will assist the superintendent in judging the true financial position of each company.
In addition to these specific proposals, the Bill would establish new rules to govern the use of reinsurance by federally-regulated insurance companies. The proposed rules, to be set by regulation, would require companies to retain a minimum portion of the business that they write. This will ensure that companies have an incentive to write good business and are not merely in existence to make money on reinsurance commissions.
Limits would also be set on the extent to which companies may reinsure business with companies that are not federally regulated, given that in the past difficulties have arisen from the inability or unwillingness of reinsurers to pay claims. Reinsurance effected with associated companies would be permitted only with the prior approval of the Superintendent. These are new and important provisions about reinsurance in this Bill. The approval of the superintendent is crucial throughout the process.

Other provisions in Bill C-56 which are concerned more specifically with the insurance sector include the authority to demand that an insurance company provide preliminary
financial statements, setting margins of assets over liabilities for small companies, provisions relating to wind-up charges and to the priority of policy holder claims when an insurance company goes bankrupt.

The next section with which I wish to deal involves securities subsidiaries which has been at the heart of the business pages and which has generated the interest of financial markets over the past two years. An important new provision in this Bill relative to its precursors is the provision to permit domestically owned, federally-regulated financial institutions to own securities dealer subsidiaries. Schedule B banks and other nonresident controlled federally-regulated financial institutions would also, with prior approval, be permitted to own a securities dealer.
In providing approval for the purchase by a non-resident of an existing dealer I remind the Flouse that the Minister would impose the condition noted in the December 18 policy statement, that not more than 50 per cent of a securities dealer could be bought prior to June 30, 1988. In the case where a new subsidiary is started the Minister would impose the condition that the subsidiary be limited to engaging in activities which its parent is permitted to do in-house. Also, where a non-resident owned institution has a Schedule B bank in Canada and wishes to purchase or establish a securities dealer, it will be required to do so through its Schedule B bank, and not independently.
In view of the conflict of interest problems which could arise with the prospect of financial institutions owning securities dealers an amendment will be proposed to Bill C-42 to ensure adequate authority for the new Superintendent of Financial Institutions to regulate the in-house securities activities of banks. This will be in addition to the measures which will be put forward in the third element of the legislative package and which were covered in the December 18 policy statement, including the creation of what are commonly known in the financial sector as "Chinese walls", greater disclosure to the consumer, and enhanced internal scrutiny through creation of a monitoring group within each institution.
The power for federal institutions to own securities dealers, as well as the constraints on the initial participation by nonresident owned institutions, are being introduced this afternoon to ensure a strong and viable Canadian presence in the strategic securities industry as it is increasingly opened to international competition. We recognize that they must be part of the international market, but we want to give them an important head start.
The final provision in the Bill about which I want to speak deals with mutual insurance companies.

Finally, another new measure is contained in a provision aimed at clarifying the residency status of mutual insurance companies. The Bill will consider as Canadian companies those mutual insurance companies whose head office and chief place

of business are located in Canada, provided three-quarters or more of the board of directors and its committees are Canadian citizens ordinarily residing in Canada.

In conclusion, I think it is clear to the House that this legislation is an important aspect of a broad, ongoing effort to bring about reform of the supervisory and regulatory framework for financial institutions in Canada. Most of the provisions have been in the public domain for several months, play a key role in strengthening supervisory powers and, if I may reiterate, were very well received by the public. By providing for more effective regulation this Bill will maintain confidence in financial institutions, an essential ingredient in maintaining a healthy financial system. As well, the Bill will allow securities markets to benefit from the provisions for ownership of securities dealers by federally-regulated institutions.
Therefore I am pleased that the House will give this matter its attention this afternoon as well as possible speedy passage into committee.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see Bill C-56 finally appear before the House. As with Bill C-42, on which I spoke earlier this month, I welcome its appearance in the House as evidence that the Government is finally beginning to move through its agenda for the reform of the financial services industry in Canada. Bill C-56 is the second of three Bills whose passage will complete the reform process which was begun by the previous Government and carried forward somewhat fitfully by the present one.
Bill C-56 was introduced on May 7. If the fact that we are starting second reading today looks remarkably and unusually speedy, I remind Hon. Members that parts of the Bill have been around in one form or another for over a year and a half. Other parts of the Bill are subject to a deadline of June 30 of this year, a deadline imposed by the need for uniformity with legislation brought forward by the Ontario Government last year when the federal Government's reform process seemed hopelessly bogged down.
The Bill is a mix of older and more recent proposals. It contains proposals that would allow federally-regulated financial institutions to own securities dealerships.
As Hon. Members know, the securities industry is provincially regulated. Obviously, it is this portion of the Bill that is meant to complement the earlier initiatives of the Ontario Government which set the effective date of June 30, 1987. However, a good part of the Bill pre-dates the White Paper issued by the Government last December. The Ontario Government's proposals to open up its securities industry were released in June, more or less obliging the Government of Canada to fall into step.
Financial Institutions
A number of the Bill's other proposals, for example the strengthening of the powers of the federal supervisory authorities and the ministerial review process for transfer of ownership, have been around for some time. On September 9, 1985, nine days after the Canadian Commercial Bank closed its doors, the then Minister of State for Finance appeared before the Finance Committee and described measures which are included in the Bill before us today. She referred to the urgent need to improve the capacity of the Government and the supervisory agencies to deal with problems in financial institutions. She described as urgent the measures she was proposing and said that they were measures on which immediate action would seem appropriate. That was in September of 1985.
Let me describe the history of those urgent measures. In November, 1985, they were released as draft legislation. In April, 1986, they were tabled as Bill C-103 respecting banks, trust and loan companies. In June, 1986, parallel measures were introduced for insurance companies in Bill C-123. These Bills were never called for debate and died on the Order Paper. In October, 1986, the measures were reintroduced as Bills C-8 and C-9. Now they have been amalgamated and lumped in with the securities proposals to form Bill C-56.
It is clear from this brief chronology that the Government is taking a bit of a liberty in including this Bill as part of its reform program. If the Government had acted with all the urgency described by the former Minister of State for Finance at the Finance Committee meeting in September of 1985, we would have had legislation in place that might have made some difference in events that later occurred in the financial services industry. At the very least, the Government might have been just a little less prone to being overtaken by events.
This Bill in fact is a collection of proposals in response to particular situations. It is in response to the bank failures, in response to the takeover of Canada Trust by a non-financial corporation, and in response to the legislative initiative of a provincial Government. This Bill did not spring from the White Paper issued in December, 1986. As I have said, it is all older than that. It is reactive rather than proactive.
This is not to say that we do not consider the Bill worthy of support. There are proposals that the Official Opposition is pleased to support since they confer what we consider necessary and desirable powers on federal regulators. This Bill would give regulators the ability to take early action against unsafe or unsound business practices by issuing cease and desist orders. Second, the Bill proposes an expansion in the regulators' powers to set and to write down the value of real estate assets held by federally-regulated financial institutions.
The power to have an independent valuation of real estate has been proven to be important because a high proportion of the assets held by financial institutions, particularly trust and loan companies, consist of real estate and mortgage loans secured by real estate. The valuation of real estate is not

Financial Institutions
always a straightforward matter and inaccurate valuations can materially affect a financial institution.
The Canadian Commercial Bank is a case in point. In the course of our hearings, the Finance Committee found that one of the factors contributing to that bank's eventual insolvency was its practice of over-valuing its loan and real estate assets. So it is appropriate for the Government to address the matter in legislation, even though we are somewhat past the point when it might have been called timely.
Another proposal in the Bill to which I alluded earlier would give the Minister the power to review and either block or give written approval to share transactions that would result in any one person or associated group acquiring more than 10 per cent of the voting shares of a financial institution. The Bill proposes that the ministerial review be based on the following criteria: first, the financial resources of the prospective purchaser; second, the purchaser's plans for the institution's future; third, the purchaser's experience and business record; and fourth, the best interests of the financial system in Canada.
It is the last criterion that concerns me. The language is unbelievably vague and imprecise. What are the best interests of the Canadian financial system? How are they to be defined and interpreted? It seems to me that the criterion of best interests as we see it in the Bill brings the matter down to a political decision in the hands of the Minister of the day. I am not satisfied to see a matter as important as the ownership of financial institutions left entirely to the discretion of any Minister.
We have heard from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) that the policy on ownership would be part of the final segment of the reform legislation. We have been told to expect a draft Bill, not a Bill, before summer. Who can say when we will have an ownership policy in place? In the meantime, we have only this Bill which says that in certain circumstances there will be a review but that the final decision will be the Minister's.
At this point I am not prepared to approve such an open-ended provision. Once this Bill is in committee, I will want to have much more information about how this provision is to be applied. In fact, my own view is that some clear criteria must be written into the legislation. I certainly would not be happy with, and I do not know of anyone else who would be, a provision that seems to say that the Minister of the day determines what constitutes the best interests of our financial system and lets the Minister have sole responsibility for deciding which large-scale transfers of control or ownership should go ahead and which should be blocked.
I turn now to the other set of proposals in Bill C-56, proposals which would permit the entry of federally-regulated financial institutions into the securities industry. As I said earlier, the Ontario Government came forward with its proposals nearly a year ago. In December, 1986, there was agreement with respect to the timetable and the effective date
of June 30, 1987. However, the introduction of the legislation before us today was delayed by a protracted dispute over what securities-related activities would fall under the jurisdiction of federal and of provincial regulators respectively. It was not until the end of April that an agreement was finally reached.
The June 30 deadline is still intact. This means that again there is pressure on us to "make quick work of this Bill in the House and in committee. There would not have been this pressure had the Government moved earlier and had the Government negotiated better.
The Bill before us today proposes to allow domestically owned financial institutions to own subsidiaries dealing in securities. Foreign banks and other foreign institutions would also be allowed to own securities dealers, subject to the approval of the Minister. Also, foreign owned institutions would be restricted to 50 per cent ownership until June 30, 1988, at which point they would be allowed 100 per cent ownership.
According to the agreement reached by the federal Government and the Ontario Government, the federal regulatory authority, that is the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, will regulate the securities related activities which are carried on directly or in-house by federally regulated financial institutions. The provincial regulator, that is the Ontario Securities Commission, will regulate all the activities of securities subsidiaries bought or established by federally regulated financial institutions.
It is clear in looking at the agreement that the parties to it were very much concerned about getting the show on the road by June 30, and that the agreement represents the very minimum of what they could find to agree upon. The accord is based very much in the here and now. It says basically that federal institutions can keep on doing in-house whatever securities activities they are doing now; anything on top of that will happen through a subsidiary which will be provincially regulated. Maybe, in the interest of short-term expediency, that is all that is needed, but surely for the long-term a more comprehensive agreement will be needed.
The agreement announced on April 27 is a bare bones affair which does not envision any change, and surely change is the one thing on which we can count as we move to a more integrated financial system in Canada.
Another concern about the agreement is that it was signed with Ontario only, with the hope that it would serve as a model for the other provinces. This is an assumption that some provinces, Alberta and Quebec in particular, are objecting to, and understandably so. After all, none of the other provinces was consulted when the Government of Canada and the Government of Ontario were negotiating. Surely the matter warrants a federal-provincial meeting and the establishment of some sort of permanent mechanism to ensure uniformity in the implementation and regulation of these new proposals which

represent significant change for the financial services industry in Canada.
We are told, according to the Bill, that foreign owned institutions wishing to enter the Canadian securities market will need the Minister's approval, but the Bill before us today does not include any criteria on which this ministerial approval would be based. Surely the Government has some criteria. However, why are they not in the Bill?
Something the federal Government should surely look for from foreign institutions wanting to enter our market is reciprocity. If foreign owned institutions are coming to compete in the Canadian market, we should be looking for equal time for our institutions on their home turf. Different countries have different financial systems, so this would have to be negotiated on a case-by-case basis. However, the principle of reciprocity should be there, and the Government should insist on it if it cares for the interests of Canadians.
I also question why the Government has chosen to allow complete foreign ownership of Canadian securities dealers when the trade negotiations with the U.S. are still ongoing. Free trade in financial services is a key part of the negotiations. Why is the Government giving up this bargaining chip now?
This was an issue that Liberal members of the Finance committee raised in our minority report in November, 1985. The committee had recommended a level playing field for domestic and foreign owned institutions in Canada; in other words, a situation of unnegotiated free trade, freely conceded. The other Liberal members on the committee and myself opposed that recommendation, saying at the time that our recommendation was to forestall changes in foreign ownership requirements until the free trade negotiating strategy had been developed and the costs and benefits of the proposals had been established. I think our recommendation is still valid today.
I should also like, before the Bill is passed, some assurance from the Government that in implementing its new system it is mindful of the possible consequences on the concentration of economic power in Canada. Concentration of assets in the financial sector is higher than in many other sectors of our economy. The Government's goal of greater integration of services can lead both to greater competitiveness and to greater concentration. It is very important to ensure that an appropriate balance is struck.
Greater integration also brings with it greater potential for abuse and conflict of interest, and thus a greater need for consistent and vigilant regulation. Bill C-56 contains a few measures in this direction, but the frustrating part is that the bulk of the new policy will be in the legislation we have yet to see.
Again I must say that I have some difficulty in assessing what is before us today when it is only a portion of the total picture. This is a criticism which I made when I spoke on Bill C-42 earlier this month. In Bill C-56 we see some proposals for transfer of ownership of financial institutions, but the over-all

ownership policy is not available to us yet in specific terms. I do not see why the Government could not have got its act together and presented us with a complete package at the outset.
Bill C-42 and Bill C-56 are welcome and useful preliminaries. However, let us be frank. The main event is yet to come and all we are hearing from the Minister with these curtain raisers is a vague promise of draft legislation.
We in the Liberal Party are willing to proceed. We are interested in getting these Bills to committee where we can explore them thoroughly and where we will have some amendments to move. However, I would certainly prefer to do so in a comprehensive fashion rather than in the piecemeal approach the Government seems to favour. I look forward to an early introduction of the remainder of the Government's proposals.

Mr. Speaker, I did not expect Bill C-56 to come forward today, but I am happy to speak on it. Of course we have already begun study of the Bill in the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs.
I realize that part of the problem with the legislation is that it is really complex. Everybody's eyes tend to glaze over, I suspect even the Minister occasionally would prefer to be watching the Stanley Cup final between the Flyers and the Oilers than to be worrying about this particular matter. He nods his head. When he writes his epitaph, hopefully some years from now-and I do not mean his political epitaph; I mean his personal epitaph-he will not put on his gravestone, "I crafted a reform of financial institutions legislation". It will be a footnote to a footnote in his biography.
Let me try to put some flesh and blood on what we are talking about in this particular Bill. We are not just talking about new rules in respect of ownership of securities firms by insurance companies and other institutions. We are not talking only about a new formula for regulation or for oversight. We are talking about a related series of Bills, Bill C-42, which we have seen, and Bill C-56, which is before us now.
The third portion-when the third shoe will drop, so to speak, which we have not yet seen and about which the Government has only given us a glimpse of its intentions-is designed to put in place a pattern or a framework of both deregulation and reregulation for Canada's financial services and banking industry. This presumably will be in force for the next 10 or 15 years. In other words, for the period from now to the turn of the century, we in this House are being asked to make decisions about major elements in the financial operations of the country.
Why is that important, Mr. Speaker? It is important because finance, the movement of money, the access to capital, the ability to gain access to the financial payments system and so on, is the lifeblood of the economy, and because in this society, as in other western capitalized democracies, the access

to political power is very closely related to access to economic power.
What we are talking about in this related series of Bills-I will talk about Bill C-56-in a somewhat broad context is the degree to which the Government of Canada will come to grips with the concentration of economic power that we have in Canada.
As I said in the debate on Bill C-42, and I repeat it now, the major weakness in what the Government is proposing is that it has not been prepared to come to grips with the excessive concentration of economic power in financial institutions and in large holding companies in Canada, and with the fact that that concentration is on the increase rather than on the decrease. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) frowns. Ele looks a bit troubled about that.
Let me read him some figures. People think that at least the major financial institutions in Canada are the chartered banks. The chartered banks of Canada are widely held. Perhaps it would surprise Hon. Members to know that the smallest of the big five financial banks-the Bank of Nova Scotia-is the eighth largest financial institution in Canada in terms of Canadian assets that it controls.
At the head of the Bank of Nova Scotia you have Power Financial Corporation, a corporation controlled by Paul Desmarais which has Canadian assets larger than those of the Bank of Nova Scotia. You have the Desjardines Group, a cooperative group, mainly centred in Quebec, based on the Caisse Populaire movement and larger than the Bank of Nova Scotia; more power to them. You have Genstar Financial Corporation, much larger than the Bank of Nova Scotia and larger than the Toronto-Dominion as well, controlled by Imasco, which if I recall correctly is in the end a British controlled conglomerate which owns 100 per cent or thereabouts of Genstar. You have Trilon Financial Corporation controlled by the Bronfmans with assets larger than either the TD Bank or the Bank of Nova Scotia. Just above them the Bank of Montreal, the Canadian Bank of Commerce and the Royal Bank of Canada.
Therefore, two of those top eight financial institutions are controlled by one or two institutions. As Diane Francis has pointed out in her excellent book on financial concentration called Controlling Interest, there is an enormous concentration of financial power in the hands of a very small number of groups. In fact, something like one-fifth of the assets of the companies on the Toronto Stock Exchange are in the hands of just a mere handful of tycoons.
I did not mention E-L Financial Corporation whose assets are just a bit below the Bank of Nova Scotia, controlled by a Toronto financier, Hal Jackman, someone also known as a prominent Tory, albeit an unsuccessful one when he has tried to run.
I am also trying to put some flesh and blood in this. We should look at the financial record of the past few years in order to see the ineffectiveness of the regulatory system which
the Government is seeking to reinforce by means of the various Bills we have before us. Half of the chartered banks in Canada have gone bust or have had to find new proprietors in the last two or three years since the Government came to power; that is one half of the schedule A banks, which is pretty bad. A whole succession of trust and insurance companies have also had very serious difficulties.
If you look at the list-I have it here-of institutions which have had particularly severe problems, Mr. Speaker, you will find a very sad and sorry tale of institutions which are now defunct, just about defunct, or have had to go on the crippled list. The list begins with the Home Bank in 1923, and jumps to 1985 with the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, not to speak of the Morguard Bank, the Bank of British Columbia and the other two banks which have had to come under new ownership. Beginning in 1980 you have Astra Trust, Fidelity Trust, AMIC Mortgage Investment Corporation, Greymac and Seaway in 1983, Northguard Mortgage Corporation in 1984, Pioneer Trust, Western Capital Trust and Continental Trust all in 1985.
Since 1976 we have seen the failures of the following federally regulated insurance companies:	Underwriters
National, American Reserve Insurance, Pitts Insurance, Strathcona General Insurance, Cardinal Insurance, Ideal Mutual Insurance and in 1985 Northumberland General Insurance Company.
What I am trying to do before coming to grips with the details of the legislation is just to remind the House and remind those dedicated readers of Hansard who will look at this debate that we are talking about real companies and real institutions which have had trouble. We are talking about real failures of the regulatory system and we are talking about concentration of ownership in the financial sector and about a Government which chooses to try to pep up the regulatory system by establishing a Superintendent of Financial Institutions but is not prepared to take any effective action to do anything about ownership.
I want to give a bit of credit to the Minister of State for Finance. He was a brave man, but his loyalty to the Cabinet is stronger than his ability or his determination to do something about the concentration of ownership. On December 4, 1986, the Minister of State took his proposals about ownership of trust companies before the Economic and Regional Development Committee of Cabinet. I cannot vouch for this because obviously I was not there. I did not have the privilege of being a fly on the wall. I hope to be in Government very soon. My Party is working at it very successfully.

only two of the largest trust companies compelling them to divest themselves of 35 per cent of their ownership over some period of time while they retain 65 per cent control. I suggest that is no discipline at all. They will still have control.

The Hon. Minister may recall the way in which the financial industry joined forces and circled the wagons when Bob Campeau of Ottawa, I suppose a constituent of mine, sought to gain control of a major trust company. Let me move on a bit. The Government of Canada has decided to join forces with the provinces, particularly the Province of Ontario. It is a bit like building the Sky Dome in Toronto. That city somehow feels inadequate if it does not have a dome stadium as extravagant and of as little potential utility as domes in other major cities.
