speechtext: What a tiny little mind you have.

There has been deregulation on Wall Street and that led to such things as a $250 million loss in mortgage security trading at Merrill Lynch. Because there was a big bang a year or so ago in London, Canada has to have its big bang, too, without looking at the evidence. When the former British Chancellor of the Exchequer, Denis Healey, was here last December he told Canadians not to do it, to learn from their mistakes. If you look at the kind of problems now being experienced on Wall Street with insider trading, massive losses in institutions which had a very good reputation, if you look at the degree to which some President Reagan's men and women are now finding a safe haven with million dollar salaries on Wall Street, I ask myself if that is what we as Canadians really want. Maybe the Minister and his colleagues in the Progressive Conservative Party want that, but I am sure there are some ordinary Canadians watching who ask whether we want a casino economy where this conglomeration of capital is perpetuated. Do we want the situation to continue where an ordinary Canadian who wants to borrow a few thousand dollars to establish a business, buy a house or expand a restaurant is put through an impossible situation by the banks.

May 29, 1987
Financial Institutions

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Talk to us, not the TV cameras.
I will talk to the citizens out there. There are only 10 Members on the other side of the Elouse but there are millions of Canadians who may be watching this particular debate.
Not since you got up.

The point I am making is that at the time when we have such a concentration of commercial interests on the boards of directors of Canadian banks, the 10 per cent ownership rule is virtually useless in undermining the concentration of economic power in our country. If I as a citizen would like to have banking services in my community until six o'clock, why do I have to wait for 25 years before the banks begin to wake up? Why is it that through most of the City of Ottawa I cannot go to a bank on a Saturday? If I happen to be in a job where I work hard from nine until six day after day, I cannot, without taking time off from my job, do my banking. When I do, I have to stand in a line with 30 other people because I happen to go on pay day because that is when I need my money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Boy, are you out of date.

How come the consumer is so badly served, yet, if I am Conrad Black and I want to do a deal and I need to bring together $500 million in bank lending, I can get that through a few telephone calls. The Hon. Member from Brampton should realize that this is precisely what is happening. There are enormous inequities in our financial system between the rich and powerful and the ordinary Canadians.
I speak, among other things, as a democratic socialist. I think there is something wrong when the Government gives to a handful of financial institutions the power to create money. For every dollar in assets they can create $ 19 or $20 by means of the credit system, as any student of economics will know. We give that privilege, and that is what it is, to our Schedule A banks. Yet do we turn around and ask whether those banks are generally doing the appropriate job for the consumer? Do we ask whether the banking services available in the Northwest Territories or in small communities are adequate? Maybe we ask but we do not get answers. In fact they are not.
Do we use the powers of the state through the Inspector General of Banks or the Superintendent of Financial Institutions in order to ensure that a consumer who is being ill-treated by the banks has some right of redress? When the banks grant a loan to Argentina and the loan fails, farmers in western Canada feel it a month or so later when suddenly credit conditions are tightened and their loans are being called. This has occurred over the course of the last few years. I express some indignation over that because I think it is appropriate from time to time that we in the House of Commons should do so and that the banks should hear some of it.
A year or two ago we had a dinner with the presidents of about five Schedule A banks. We had a very jolly time, I and members of my caucus who had taken pains to meet with the banks. It was a very interesting session. We talked about a number of things including concerns the NDP has over the adequacy of services for farmers and small business people. It is really a scandal at times the way some of those people are dealt with. While in general there are aspects to our banking system which are more favourable and more effectively operated than in other countries, I asked why in a country where 40 per cent of the workforce are members of trade unions, you and your institutions have moved heaven and earth to keep the union out of your institutions? There was such a frost that descended on that cosy little tete-a-tete-I had accepted a couple of glasses of wine from the bankers in the interests of communication-you could almost see the icicles hanging down from the walls. I have real concerns about giving privileges to those large financial institutions when they turn around and give generously to the Progressive Conservatives and the Liberals.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: You would not accept it.

They do their bit to keep men and women working for financial institutions in a subservient way. They should be ashamed of the way they have behaved over the course of the last two or three decades. They have denied working men and women the right to speak for themselves and are basically trying to perpetuate the labour-employer relationships of the 19th century. Those are the facts. That is how those institutions have been operating.
I say all these things to put what we are talking about into perspective. We as parliamentarians and legislators should be very aware of the abuses which have taken place in our financial institutions. Just because banks do a few good things as corporate citizens we should not be blinded to the fact that there has been too much self-dealing and concentration of ownership. Neither the United States nor Japan allow their banks to engage in underwriting, yet we are about to do that. That is very serious.
What would happen, for example, if we had another Dome situation and the banks or their security subsidiaries are involved in underwriting equity or debt for a new Dome Petroleum? Will the banks which will be concerned about their loans to that particular institution turning bad tell their security people to sell a bit of equity because they are feeling shaky about it? What kind of Chinese wall could prevent the potential abuses in such a situation? All we will get is a Chinese wall based on soft noodles which will not prevent that kind of abuse from taking place.
In the context of the present negotiations for free trade with the United States one must ask whether the United States has offered to allow Canadian banks to own securities subsidiaries in the United States. For 30 or 40 years they have insisted on
May 29, 1987

strict segregation and they will not change just because Canada says it should be so. We are saying that as of this June any American bank can own and have effective control of a securities house here in Canada. As of June, 1988, they will be able to have 100 per cent ownership.
If I were running a $20 billion bank in the United States I would very quickly take advantage of this opportunity and buy a subsidiary here in Canada. We are likely to give American banks a back door to the securities market and then the subsidiary of the Canadian firm will do business in the United States. That is a perfectly logical thing to do.
The other day I said that the investment dealers in this country are like the chickens going to Colonel Sanders because they do not realize that we are seeing the end of an independent securities industry in Canada. As a democratic socialist I am not sure if I should leap to their defence. I noticed that the spokesman from Nesbitt Thomson was beginning to wake up to that fact the other day, but the investment dealers are too late. They have been sold out.
There are some very serious questions which still have not been adequately answered with regard to the degree to which the Government has moved into this area with the consent of Ontario but no particular agreement from the other provinces. We will have to explore in committee where that will lead, but I have some grave reservations about the way in which it has proceeded.
I want to talk now in more specific terms about the Bill and some concerns which New Democrats have about financial services in general. I have been developing some policy, as is appropriate for an opposition spokesman. I suggest to the Minister that there is an over-emphasis on the problems of stability. It is not that those problems are not real, but they are addressed too much by regulation rather than ownership. The missing element is that we are not at all taking up the needs of consumers. That is a real question in that too many banks still close at three o'clock. It is a real question if consumers have to pay an inordinate rate of interest.
An example of the abuse in a supposedly competitive area is that it took the Commons Finance Committee two months to persuade the chartered banks to lower interest rates and service fees on credit cards to a more reasonable level. It was clear that they were making excessive profits and they have now agreed to roll them back. However, a Common's committee should not be responsible for ensuring that kind of protection. It should be there at all times. There should be a means by which individual consumers, small businessmen, farmers and so on can have their grievances against banks examined and get some redress.
The drafting problems in Bill C-56 are very serious. For example, it amends sections of the Canada British Insurance Act which are being amended simultaneously through Bill C-42. I have to ask who is smoking what in the drafting section of the Ministry of Finance.
Financial Institutions
I disagree with banks having security underwriting powers, but the proprietors of the Montreal District Savings Bank point out that if the chartered banks are to have those powers, surely the Quebec Savings Bank Act should be suitably amended as well. If we are going to make a wrong decision, we should not put the City and District Savings Bank on a basis different from that of the co-operative institutions, the financial institutions, and the chartered banks.
With respect to securities regulations in general, we should be seriously looking at a form of joint agency. The present situation in which the provinces all go their own way is ludicrous in a country of 25 million. I would have liked to have seen more leadership from the Government on this. I am sorry that it has not been forthcoming. We have retained an awkward compromise with the securities commission in Ontario doing the job of a national securities commission while Quebec, Alberta and other jurisdictions are able to pass independent legislation. I realize that we will not get a federal securities commission which is under provincial jurisdiction, but there is enough overlapping jurisdiction, particularly as the pillars collapse, that I think the Government, even now, could be taking initiative to get a joint body in which both levels of Government might give up some powers to get a common pattern of securities regulation. My Party does not believe that just because there has been a big bang in London or on Wall Street we have to follow that particular route.
The Bill speaks specifically to the moratorium on ownership.
I think that section is ludicrous in the absence of any adequate ownership rules. The guidelines which include the stipulation that the Minister must look at the best interests of the financial system are meaningless. I do not know what the devil they mean. If I were the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) I might say that it is in the best interests of the financial system not to have further concentration of ownership and, therefore, reject any share transfer which would involve the passage of control of a widely held financial institution into narrower hands. It could be argued that that would be an abuse of a very wide paragraph. I think the whole section is rather nuts. It disguises the Government's failure to come to grips with the ownership powers.
With regard to the cease and desist powers in Bill C-56, the Government is giving the Superintendent of Financial Institutions the power to move in and exercise the powers of directors for a short period of time without giving the institution any power to retaliate or resist and then, with ministerial approval, to do it on a more permanent basis. I believe one can make a strong case that something like that might have been useful in the events we have experienced over the last few years. It is also fair to say, that had there been the will to act on behalf of the regulators, there would be no need for the legislation. It was the failure of will, both at the official level and at the ministerial level which, in large measure, accounts for the approximately $2 billion we had to pay out through the CDIC and, in other ways, over the course of the last couple of years.

May 29, 1987
Financial Institutions
The point I want to make is that I think there are real problems in terms of information being available to other than insiders. I cited in committee the other day an example. Let us suppose that I was a small entrepreneur, I was a good socialist developer and was about to develop a few factory units or a small shopping centre. Socialists do these things as well, Mr. Speaker. The Minister seems to be a bit upset. Suppose I arranged for insurance with a company and the insurance was the last element in making my deal fly. Suppose that three days before I signed the contract with the agent for the insurance company, the Superintendent of Financial Institutions had moved in because he had reason to believe the insurance company was about to belly-up. I took my risks, I committed my capital, without that knowledge. Then it became evident a few days later, after I had signed the contracts and committed my capital, that the insurance had unravelled. With the insurance unravelled, the deal unravelled and I found myself completely up the creek.
The question is, at what point is information to be made available publicly? That is an issue with which we will be dealing in committee. I think it is a very serious issue because if the Superintendent has grounds to move into a company, it seems to me there has to be some way by which that information can be made public.
The Ontario Securities Commission and the SCC in the United States make their actions public despite the fact that those actions will have an effect on the quoted market value of shares actually being traded at that time. We have to look at that and perhaps get used to it.
The point was made about the appraisal of asset values. Again, the Government has failed to address the responsibility of accountants and auditors in this particular area. In other words, they will advise in an area where they have in many respects been a cause of the problems with which we are concerned.
The committee is concerned, and I put this to the Minister now, over the fact that the limits on reinsurance are being put down by regulation when in fact it is appropriate, because it is such a major restraint on the operations of an insurance company, that at least the broad parameters should be in the legislation itself and just in the form of regulations.
With respect to the insurance companies, there is also a matter of consumer protection. The Minister, coming from Ontario and a community where insurance is an important industry, will know the concern which my colleague, Bob Rae, a former Member of this House and Leader of my Party in Ontario, has been raising over the degree to which property and casualty companies are bleeding Ontario drivers dry with the rates they are charging for automobile insurance. In particular, we are concerned about the way in which they are abusing individuals because of arbitrary rules which in some cases have driven businesses to the wall. For example, there was a case in the papers the other day of a woman who
married her boyfriend-I think she was probably living with him as well-and as a consequence, the insurance she had to pay on her vehicle rose from $600 to $1500, just like that. The fact that she assured the insurance company that her husband was not going to drive her vehicle was irrelevant. That kind of silliness has to stop.
Just as there is a desirability for the federal Government in respect to banks to protect the consumer, I think there should be a measure of consumer protection as well with respect to insurance companies who also have the privilege, not the right, of carrying out insurance duties here in Canada.
Talk to Bob Ray. It is a provincial issue.

The Minister says it is a provincial issue. If these companies are federally regulated, then I believe we can in fact provide some direction in terms of how those companies are to operate. If people then choose to set up provincially regulated insurance companies because they do not like the federal rules, that is fine. Let the province deal with them. But I do not think we as federal legislators should abdicate our responsibility in that particular area.
There are a number of specific points which perhaps I will have a chance to talk about later. However, I would like to make a point to the Minister in a very serious way. What we have heard from the officials of the Department of Finance with respect to the resources which will be made available to the new Superintendent of Financial Institutions is extremely disturbing.
The previous Inspector General of Banks should have, in my opinion, put his job on the line to get adequate resources to do his job as Inspector General. It is a personal tragedy, I think, that he did not have the gumption to do so perhaps five or six years ago. He did not and his office was too weak. He perhaps lacked some of the will to do what he needed to do and that contributed to the failures of the banks which we have experienced.
What senior officials of the Department of Finance have told us is that there will only be a moderate increase in the resources which will be made available to the office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions relative to what was available to the Inspector of Insurance and to the Inspector General of Banks.
That's not true.

The Minister says that this is not true. I hope he will answer that in committee since he will not have a chance to answer here in the House. That is a very serious concern, particularly in view of the excessive reliance on regulations which my Party has indicated we believe is contained in the Act.
I would like to suggest that part of the changes in corporate governments-and perhaps that is still to come-should include a broader reflection of the community on boards of directors for financial institutions. These boards should include
May 29, 1987

representation for consumers, farmers, small business, women and other relevant groups. That is something which 1 think we can insist upon because these institutions operate not by right, but because of a privilege which is given to them in the powers of limited liability, the powers to create money and the other powers they have under federal legislation. We are very concerned about the degree to which self-dealing is permitted. We are concerned about the degree to which there is a total deregulation of the power of making commercial loans by nonfinancial institutions.
These are some of the points about which we are particularly concerned. I could make other points but I guess I will just conclude by saying that we should have addressed, in the reform of the financial institutions, a number of consumer issues as well as the stabilities issues so that the way in which those institutions offer services to consumers was addressed, and there was some redress for consumers. There is a very serious need for a kind of financial ombudsman who would be on the consumer's side.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NON-SMOKERS' HEALTH ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, March 31, consideration of the motion of Ms. McDonald that Bill C-204, an Act to regulate smoking in the federal workplace and on common carriers and to amend the Hazardous Products Act in relation to cigarette advertising, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NON-SMOKERS' HEALTH ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to join the debate today on Bill C-204. As the only actuary elected to the House I would like to begin by commending the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for bringing this important initiative forward, and to indicate that I intend to support the Bill on second reading. However, I should also signal that if the Bill were to leave the legislative committee unamended, I would be forced to vote against it as it currently stands at third reading.
The Bill contains several important features. The first feature would restrict smoking at the work station. I support this feature of the Bill. However, the Bill also provides that designated smoking rooms should be provided for employees who wish to continue to smoke at the office, and imposes a stipulation that any such room be both enclosed and independently ventilated.
While I have no particular objections to the designated smoking room concept per se, I cannot justify the allocation of several hundred millions of taxpayers' dollars at this time to provide for independently ventilated smoking rooms in many old buildings used by the Public Service. It may be desirable, however, to consider such a feature for buildings designed in the future. For this reason, if the Bill passes second reading, and if the independent ventilation feature remains in the Bill, I would oppose it at third reading.
The Bill would also restrict smoking on airplanes, ships, railways and motor vehicles under federal jurisdiction. This feature of the Bill goes far beyond what was recently announced by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) who restricted smoking only on airplane flights of less than two hours' duration. I believe that the proposals of the Bill to consider further limitations on smoking on common carriers are worth future study. It is principally for this reason that I offer my support for the Bill at this time.
Finally, the Bill would designate tobacco and tobacco products under the Hazardous Products Act. As an actuary there is no doubt in my mind that tobacco is a hazardous product. I would like to see committee hearings held to establish whether such a designation would be in the public

May 29, 1987
Non-Smokers' Health Act
interest and what the ramifications of such a designation would be.
The debate concerning the use of tobacco is an old one. The first reference I was able to find described tobacco as "barbarous, beastly, hateful to the nose, a vile and stinking custom, harmful to the brain, and dangerous to the lungs". The comment, I hasten to add, was not made by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood but by King James I in the year 1604.
Nevertheless, tobacco-related illnesses did not begin to flourish until the invention of the cigarette machine in 1880. In that year, 500 million cigarettes were produced commercially in the United States. Within five years the production doubled to one billion cigarettes; and within another five years the production quadrupled to four billion cigarettes. Some 90 years later, in 1980, the annual production of cigarettes in the United States was 620 billion and in Canada it was about 64 billion.
Almost all Canadians know of the association of smoking with lung cancer. What most people do not know is that lung cancer was almost unknown prior to the invention of the cigarette machine. At the turn of the century the pathologist Adler estimated in a review of world hospitals that he had been able to uncover that only about 300 cases of lung cancer had ever been reported. Today, it is the number one killer in terms of cancer for males. In one hospital in Toronto alone, the Princess Margaret, there were 1,119 new cases of lung cancer in 1980.
Cigarette smoking is now the number one cause of premature death in North America. Actuarial studies indicate that it is responsible for 33 per cent of all cancer deaths, 25 per cent of all coronary heart disease deaths, and 40 per cent of all respiratory disease deaths.
Not only do smokers die early, they are sick more frequently. Smokers are hospitalized 50 per cent more than nonsmokers. They have twice the accident rate of non-smokers. It is estimated that in 1980 dollars each smoker costs an employer an average of $600 in lost productivity.
Actuaries have been studying mortality differences between smokers and non-smokers since 1964. The ratio of smoker to non-smoker mortality among insured lives is 15 times higher for respiratory cancer, 14.7 times higher for pneumonia and influenza, 8.1 times higher for hypertensive heart disease, and 5.8 times higher for fatal digestive diseases.
In the United States a detailed mortality study of all U.S. veterans has been conducted. In addition to the elevated rates of cancers of the lung and bronchia mentioned above it was found that smokers are 12.5 times more likely to contract cancer of the pharynx, 10 times more likely to contract cancer of the larynx, 6.2 times more likely to contract cancer of the oesophagus, and 5.2 times more likely to have an aortic aneurysm.
Over the study period 1960 to 1984, it is estimated that 659,000 Canadians had premature deaths directly related to tobacco use-almost 30,000 a year. Studies indicate that the extra mortality is directly related to the age that a person first began smoking, as well as the number of cigarettes smoked per day. This is why it is so important to control the new use of smoking among our youth and why I support the recent ban on tobacco advertising introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp).
However, there is some hope for smokers. Studies also indicate that mortality starts to return to normal after smoking stops. For those who smoke less than an average of 20 cigarettes a day mortality is only 30 per cent above normal after one year of abstinence and is essentially back to normal after 10 years of abstinence.
Those who smoke more than a pack a day are not quite so lucky. Their mortality in the year after they stopped smoking is still 269 per cent of normal. However, after 10 years even heavy user mortality drops to only 50 per cent above normal. This 50 per cent figure is as high as it is because it includes a large number of people who quit smoking on doctors' orders because they had already developed severe health problems.
If one were to study former heavy smokers who quit voluntarily before their doctors told them to one would find that their mortality is quite close to normal within five years and is essentially back to normal within 10 years. Unfortunately, those who wait until the doctor orders them to quit smoking have considerably elevated mortality even 15 years after they stop smoking, that is those who are still alive.
The actuarial statistical studies are numerous and consistent. Tobacco use kills. Tobacco use disables. Even indirect smoke inhaled by a non-smoker is dangerous. Tobacco use is a health menace. It is now socially unacceptable to expose others to the risks of second-hand smoke at the office or on public transit.
Once again, I wish to congratulate the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood for bringing forward Bill C-204. Obviously, she has served to focus Parliament's attention on the most serious health problem we have in Canada.
Within the last few weeks the Government has taken major initiatives to curtail smoking. Hopefully, by passage of this Bill at second reading and study in committee several additional reasonable steps can be found which might save additional hundreds of lives a year.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NON-SMOKERS' HEALTH ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), on an excellent and very topical Bill. It deals with a subject matter which is foremost in the minds of many Canadians. My colleague, the Hon. Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan), brought out a great many statistics which I think are worthwhile and which should be considered by all Canadians. I would like to talk generally about the Bill for a long time, but there are some specific matters I would like to bring forward.
May 29, 1987

Bill C-204 which is in its final hour of debate today addresses two specific areas related to the use of tobacco products in Canada. First, it seeks to restrict smoking in federally-regulated workplaces, transit vehicles and other locations under federal jurisdiction. Second, it would ban the advertising and promotion of cigarettes. The goals of this Bill are indeed laudable.
The detrimental effects of tobacco smoke, not only on the health of smokers but also on the health of non-smokers who may be forced to breathe air contaminated with tobacco smoke, has been clearly established. It would therefore be unconscionable on our part to ignore this problem.
On April 22 of this year the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) announced major new initiatives concerning the use of tobacco products in Canada. I shall concentrate on one particular aspect of these initiatives and that is, the issue of smoking in the workplace.
There are approximately 900,000 workers in the federal jurisdiction. The Minister of Labour has the responsibility of ensuring that the health and safety of these workers are protected while they are in the workplace. He fulfils that responsibility by administering the Canada Labour Code. Part IV of the Code addresses the issues of occupational safety and health.
There are two specific points in the Code which the Minister of Labour is intending to use in order to minimize the exposure of workers to second-hand smoke. The first point concerns the creation of joint health and safety committees. These committees are mandatory for establishments with 20 or more employees. A safety and health representative is required and the committees are composed of representatives of both employees and management.
The Minister proposes to request employers to restrict smoking in their workplaces to specifically designated areas. This is to be implemented by the employers in full consultation with their safety and health committees or safety and health representatives as the case may be and should be in place before the end of 1987. This is phase one of his initiatives.
The second point is the authority that the Code bestows on the Minister of Labour to prescribe specific regulations pertaining to any aspect of the occupational safety and health of workers under federal jurisdiction. Phase two of his initiatives involves the development of a new regulation regarding smoking in the workplace.
At the present time, the Minister's Department is actively engaged in a full-scale technical review of all aspects of the Canada occupational and safety and health regulations issued pursuant to Part IV of the Canada Labour Code. This review is being carried out in an unique way which I consider to be very Canadian. A special review committee has been set up
Non-Smokers' Health Act
with the joint participation of labour and industry representatives.
The Minister will be requesting this committee to develop the regulation on smoking and to have it ready to take effect in 1989. He has publicly announced his hope that the review committee will seriously consider a total ban on smoking in all federally-regulated workplaces. The highlight of these initiatives by the Minister of Labour is the active participation of the two key stakeholders in this issue, employers and employees.
We all know that the practice of smoking dates back many centuries and it has become well entrenched in the daily habits of millions of Canadians. We are debating an issue that constitutes a major lifestyle change for these Canadians. Surely, unless we can get the co-operation and good will of both smoking and non-smoking workers, our efforts will be in vain.
One reasonable way of minimizing this potential hazard in the workplace is by seeking the co-operation of employers and employees. This is precisely what the Minister of Labour intends to do. Unfortunately, it is not altogether clear that Bill C-204 would involve employers and employees in the process of decision-making and implementation of workplace smoking restrictions. Experience has shown that when employers and employees are involved in the design and implementation of workplace smoking policies, the policies that result work well and are self-enforcing.
According to Bill C-204, a workplace is considered smoke-free if the concentration of airborne tobacco tar in that space does not exceed .75 micrograms per cubic metre of air. In my opinion, this issue can be more easily addressed by administrative action, and that is precisely the route the Minister of Labour is taking at the moment.
I am sure we all appreciate the complexity of this problem. I am convinced that the phased-in approach put forward by the Minister of Labour will succeed in reducing this hazard to the health of Canadians. In conclusion, let me once again give credit to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood, for bringing this issue to the forefront. I would urge my fellow Hon. Members, however, to consider the major initiatives taken by the Government in deciding how its members will eventually vote on Bill C-204.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NON-SMOKERS' HEALTH ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on an important Private Member's Bill which has attracted a great deal of attention in my riding and, I am sure, across Canada.
The Government which I support has taken an active role over the past two years in addressing the issue of cigarette smoking. This has been in response to overwhelming evidence that tobacco smoke is the largest preventable cause of illness and premature death in Canada. Moreover, it is becoming increasingly clear that Canadians who are consistently exposed to smoke in the environment may also be suffering adverse health effects. Not surprisingly, the public is increasingly

May 29, 1987
Non-Smokers' Health Act
asking for an environment that protects non-smokers from tobacco smoke.
The effects of direct exposure to smoke have been clearly demonstrated over the past decades. Thirty per cent of cancer deaths, 30 per cent of heart disease deaths, and 90 per cent of chronic obstructive lung disease deaths are caused by tobacco. More than 30,000 Canadians die each year from smoking-related diseases and 17 per cent of all deaths in Canada are attributed to smoking.
The evidence on the effects of environmental or passive smoking has only begun to emerge in the past 10 years or so. Research to date indicates a relationship between passive smoke and low birth weight and injury for unborn babies, respiratory illnesses for children and lung cancer for those involuntarily exposed to smoke over a long period of time such as spouses of smokers.
The U.S. Surgeon General estimates that one hour spent by non-smokers in a smoke-filled room my be equivalent to their smoking five to thirty cigarettes. In his 1986 annual report, he recommended that exposure to environmental tobacco smoke be eliminated and that policies aiming to do this be implemented with the input and support of all involved including smokers and non-smokers and management and employees.
I would like to comment briefly on the recent initiatives announced by the Government to reduce tobacco use in Canada, and particularly those measures to reduce smoking in the federal government workplace. As part of the Government's initiatives which were referred to by my friend from Scarborough and announced on April 22, 1987, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) indicated his intention to declare a ban on smoking in all Public Service workplaces by January 1, 1989. This smoking ban will be implemented in a phased-in manner based on consultation with the unions in the National Joint Council. This consultation is essential to achieve the successful and harmonious implementation of a ban and to ensure the continued co-operation and compliance of all employees.
The Public Service of Canada is the largest employer under federal jurisdiction and has a number of unique work situations and work sites. Some work sites are shared with employees of private sector employers, others are the full-time residents of special client groups or of Public Service employees, and some work sites are in shared accommodations with the general public. These situations will need to be considered and addressed in the consultation process to establish implementation measures that take into account these special situations.
There are already a number of Public Service departments that have restricted smoking in their workplaces. These measures were implemented after consultation with the employees involved. The experiences of these departments indicate that not only non-smokers but also many smokers and in fact the majority of smokers among the employees supported these initiatives.
It is increasingly evident that smoking in the workplace and in other public areas is becoming unacceptable to a majority of Canadians. The Government's initiative to ban smoking in the Public Service workplace reflects the rapidly changing public and employee attitudes toward tobacco usage. Daily we hear of employers implementing bans or restricting smoking in the workplace to a few designated, agreed upon smoking areas. Exposure to second-hand tobacco smoke in the workplace is no longer tolerated and employees have requested action on this issue.
In 1985, Treasury Board, in consultation with Public Service unions, developed guidelines to assist Departments in implementing measures to control smoking in the workplace. Certain areas were identified where public servants could not smoke, for example in areas or at service counters where the general public was served. It was agreed at that time that the guidelines were an interim measure designed to inform Departments of the increasing sensitivity to this issue and of the need to consult with their employees on ways to resolve cooperatively differences related to tobacco smoke in the workplace. It was also agreed that these guidelines were for a period of three years and that thereafter a more stringent approach would be required. Both the Treasury Board and the unions in the National Joint Council agreed to start consulting on a standard a year ahead of schedule because of increasing pressure to have more stringent measures apply.
According to Health and Welfare Canada, the successful implementation of a smoking ban is based upon strong support for a ban by the senior management of an organization and consultation with employees on the development of a phased in plan to achieve this ban. These measures, as I have indicated, are being adopted by the Public Service of Canada.
The announcement of the Government's intention to ban smoking in the Public Service workplace is an important and progressive step by Canada's largest employer. It is hoped that it may serve as a catalyst for other employers.

speechtext: It is the second one.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NON-SMOKERS' HEALTH ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I beg your pardon. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) has corrected me.
The Bill calls for two measures-first, to ban advertising by declaring tobacco to be a hazardous product and, second, to ban smoking in federally regulated workplaces, particularly in the Government of Canada.
May 29, 1987

I was pleased that the Government had finally began to act on this issue and that it announced some policy in this area in the press conference held by the Minister of National Elealth and Welfare (Mr. Epp) about four weeks or five weeks ago.
Elowever, I was disappointed by two aspects of the Government's proposal. The first is that the proposed advertising ban is incomplete. It will continue to allow point of sale advertising. I think it is well known that if one stifles advertising in one way but leaves a loophole, the advertising funds-and I believe that they amount to $200 million per year which cannot be spent elsewhere-will go into the area which is still exempt. In other words, we are likely to see a substantial increase in point of sale advertising, which will continue to communicate the idea that it is hip, smart, sexy, or somehow positive to be seen with a cigarette in one's mouth.
Second, tobacco companies, perhaps by registering subsidiaries with the names of their brand in the title, will be able to promote their products in terms of sporting and other types of events which they help to sponsor. There too I have some real questions. To have Macdonald Export establish a subsidiary so that it can subsidize the Macdonald Export ballet or some such event is another covert way by which promotion and public relations on behalf of cigarette smoking are likely to be permitted. It is a shame.
Another problem with the Minister's Bill is the fact that he lacks urgency and is not prepared to act in what I believe is the spirit of the Elouse when it decided to put in force a procedure to allow Private Members' Bills to come to vote. If the Minister were really seized with the urgency, I believe he should have in fact said: "I will piggyback the Government's proposals on to the Bill proposed by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood". We all know that parliamentary time is very scarce. It is difficult for measures or for Bills to actually get heard.
If the Minister were sincere in wanting his Bill or his proposals to go before a committee as rapidly as possible, it seems to me that he should have agreed to see the Bill go and, if his Party had amendments, it could have made its amendments and let the committee do what it would with the particular proposals.
It is no secret that I support the Bill. I am an ex-smoker. I quit in 1983, on New Year's Eve. It was a New Year's resolution which I have actually succeeded in maintaining. I am still scared to death that if I ever had one cigarette, I would be hooked by the habit again. I believe it is an addiction which lasts through life.
I am pleased with the support the Bill has attracted. Three or four groups have written letters of endorsement which I should like to put on record. One is from Frank Garritty, President of the Canadian Teachers' Federation, and is directed to the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood. It reads:
I am pleased to advise that, at its most recent meeting, the Board of Directors
of the Canadian Teachers' Federation passed a resolution endorsing Bill C-
204. The Canadian Teachers' Federation represents 220,000 elementary and
Non-Smokers' Health Act
secondary school teachers who teach in every province and territory of Canada.
Another one is from Ginette Rodger, Executive Director of the Canadian Nurses Association. It is directed to the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood and reads:
The Canadian Nurses Association .. . supports your initiative in bringing this Private Member's Bill. The CNA Board of Directors has reviewed the Bill and has reacted very favourably. The Board is concerned however that the occupational health hazard created by smoking is so significant that smoking should be banned in all federal government workplaces.
Another one is from Wendy Williams, Vice-President of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. She wrote to the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood as follows:
On behalf of Canadian women who are members of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, thank you for Bill C-204.
We hope this Act, to regulate smoking in the federal workplace and on common carriers and to amend the Hazardous Products Act in relation to cigarette advertising, gets discussed and passed in the House of Commons.
The last letter is from Bob White, National President of CAW. It is dated March 24, 1987 and it is addressed to the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood. It reads:
-I want to congratulate you on the work you have done towards guaranteeing Canadian workers a tobacco smoke-free environment-there can be no justification for any delay in passing legislation controlling it. It is for this reason that we whole-heartedly endorse your Private Member's Bill, the NonSmokers' Health Act-C-204.
This letter was from CAW, one of the most important unions in the country. These are only some of the more recent letters endorsing this particular measure.
I remind Hon. Members that we are dealing with a health hazard which results in the direct death of some 35,000 people per year. To put it into perspective, I should like to refer to some figures from the Canadian Council on Smoking and Health. It is equivalent in 18 months to the total number of Canadian servicemen and servicewomen who were killed in World War II. In other words, tobacco is creating as much death and suffering every 18 months as Canada experienced as a nation from its participation in World War II.
The costs are enormous. It is time that we took action in order to indicate that tobacco no longer has the endorsement or approval, either in a direct or in a covert way, of the Government of Canada.
If some manufacturer said to the Department of National Health and Welfare that it had a great new product which it wanted to make available to Canadians, which would send hundreds of thousands of them to hospital, which would shorten their life spans from seven years to eight years on average, and which would cause 35,000 deaths every year; if some manufacturer asked "would you please allow me to sell this product in Canada", we would all say it was appalling. However, that is precisely what we continue to allow because of the degree to which Canadians have permitted the tobacco manufacturers' lobby to dictate what we should do.
We have alternative uses for the farmland affected. We, as Canadians, should be prepared to put up some of the money

May 29, 1987
Non-Smokers' Health Act
saved by the reduction in smoking to ensure that tobacco farmers can phase into other areas. Neither the manufacturers, the employees, nor the farmers have a compelling case that we should continue with this health hazard and make it as publicly available as we do now when it causes such amounts of illness, death, carnage, and loss of life as tobacco does today.
This is why I believe that all Members of Parliament should support Bill C-204. Once again I congratulate the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood on what I think is a very positive contribution. I also note with a great deal of approval the way in which members of all Parties have endorsed the Bill and the degree to which even the Minister of National Health and Welfare has now joined in publicly condemning the health hazards caused by tobacco smoking.
It is a disease. It is an illness. We should do away with it. In 50 years we will wonder how anybody could have put a stick of tobacco in his or her mouth. It is time we brought it to an end.
